knowledge-base.overview: Testing depth practices covering the testing pyramid, AAA pattern, isolation, what to test, contract testing for microservices, mutation testing, and test data patterns. Complements knowledge/testing.xml which covers framework-specific setup.

level.name: Unit tests
level.description: Test a single function, method, or class in complete isolation. All dependencies are replaced with fakes or stubs.
level.speed: Milliseconds per test — the whole suite runs in seconds
level.when-to-use: For all business logic, calculations, transformations, validations, and decision branches

level.name: Integration tests
level.description: Test one integration boundary at a time: your code talking to a real database, a real HTTP client, a real file system. Not UI, not end-to-end.
level.speed: Seconds per test — the suite runs in minutes
level.when-to-use: For repository layers, external service clients, message queue producers/consumers

level.name: End-to-end tests
level.description: Test a complete user journey through the deployed system, including UI or the outermost API.
level.speed: Slow — seconds to minutes per test, brittle to environment changes
level.when-to-use: For the most critical user flows only: login, checkout, core workflow. Not for every edge case.

why-this-shape.reason: Unit tests are cheap to write, fast to run, easy to maintain, and pinpoint failures precisely.
E2E tests are slow, brittle, hard to debug, and require a full running environment. Adding more of them slows the feedback loop.
Integration tests balance coverage and speed — they catch wiring problems without the brittleness of full E2E.
Push testing as far down the pyramid as possible. If you can test a behavior with a unit test, do that — not an integration test.

ice-cream-anti-pattern.description: The inverted pyramid (ice cream cone): mostly E2E tests, few unit tests. Common in legacy codebases with no DI or abstraction.
ice-cream-anti-pattern.symptoms: Test suite takes 30+ minutes. Tests fail randomly. Developers avoid running tests locally.
ice-cream-anti-pattern.fix: Introduce dependency injection, extract business logic from framework code, write unit tests for extracted logic.

aaa-pattern.description: Structure every test with three clearly separated phases: Arrange, Act, Assert.

phases.phase: Set up the preconditions: create objects, configure mocks, seed data, set up the initial state. Everything the system needs before the action happens.
Execute exactly one action: call the method under test, trigger the event, send the HTTP request. If you're calling multiple things in Act, you may be testing too much.
Verify the outcome: check return values, verify mock interactions, inspect state changes. Keep assertions focused — test one behavior per test.

rules.rule: Keep each phase short. If Arrange is 30 lines, extract a builder or factory method.
One Act per test. If you're calling the method under test twice, split into two tests.
Prefer one Assert per test, or a small set of closely related assertions. Multiple unrelated assertions mean multiple test cases.
Test names are documentation. They should tell you what behavior is being verified without reading the test body.
Name tests after behavior, not after the internal implementation. "should_apply_discount" not "calls_discount_calculator".
If a test name needs "and" in it, it's probably two tests.
Avoid generic names: Test1, TestHappyPath, TestMethod. These communicate nothing.
Tests must not depend on each other. Any test must pass when run in isolation or in any order.
Tests must not share mutable state. Reset all state in setup/teardown, or create fresh objects per test.
Tests must not depend on external services in production (real databases, real APIs, real message queues) unless they are explicitly integration tests.
Never rely on test execution order. If Test B only passes when Test A runs first, you have a hidden dependency.

isolation-styles.rule: Use solitary tests when collaborators are heavy or have side effects. Use sociable tests when involving real collaborators gives more meaningful coverage.

fakes.type: Returns canned responses. Used in Arrange to control inputs to the system under test.
Records interactions. Used in Assert to verify the system under test called something the right way.
A working implementation with simplified behavior (e.g., in-memory repository). Better than mocks for complex scenarios.
A real object that records calls. Use sparingly — can couple tests to implementation.
fakes.rule: Prefer stubs and fakes over mocks. Overusing mocks couples tests to implementation details.

what-to-test.rule: Test behavior through the public interface, not internal implementation. If tests only pass by calling private methods, the class may need splitting.
Test what the system does (outputs, side effects, state changes), not how it does it (which internal methods are called).
Skip trivial code: simple getters/setters with no logic, pure pass-through delegations. They add noise and break on every rename.
Test all non-trivial branches: happy path, expected error cases, edge cases (null, empty, boundary values, overflow).
If you feel compelled to test a private method, it's a signal that the class is doing too much. Extract it into a separate testable class.

good-tests.test: Verifies return values or output state
Verifies that expected side effects happen (message sent, event published)
Verifies that unexpected side effects don't happen
Verifies that correct exceptions are thrown for invalid input

bad-tests.test: Verifies internal call sequences ("verify OrderService calls DiscountCalculator.apply() twice")
Tests framework behavior (don't test that ASP.NET routing works)
Tests against constants rather than meaningful values (Assert.Equal(MAGIC_NUMBER, result) with no explanation)

contract-testing.description: For microservices, contract testing verifies that a consumer's expectations of a provider's API are met, without requiring a full integration environment.

consumer-driven-contracts.rule: The consuming service writes tests expressing what it expects from the provider API: which endpoints, what request shape, what response shape.
These expectations are captured in a "pact file" (machine-readable contract).
The providing service runs the pact file as part of its CI, verifying it can satisfy the consumer's requirements.
If the provider changes an endpoint in a way that breaks the contract, the CI fails — catching the break before deployment.
consumer-driven-contracts.tool: Pact is the standard tool for this. It generates JSON pact files from consumer tests and runs them as provider verification.

workflow.step: 1. Consumer team writes CDC tests defining expected requests/responses
2. Pact generates a pact file from those tests
3. Pact file is published to a Pact Broker (shared registry)
4. Provider CI fetches the pact file and runs provider verification tests
5. Provider verification result is published back to the Pact Broker
6. Both teams can deploy independently when verification passes

benefits.benefit: Teams can refactor provider internals freely as long as the contract passes
Catches API breaking changes before they reach production
Eliminates the need for a shared staging environment for contract validation
Creates a living specification of what each consumer needs

mutation-testing.description: Mutation testing measures the quality of your test suite, not just its coverage. It makes small deliberate bugs (mutations) in your code and checks whether your tests catch them.

how-it-works.step: The tool (Stryker, PIT, Mutmut) creates thousands of copies of your code, each with one small change: flipping a > to >=, removing a null check, changing a + to -.
It runs your test suite against each mutated copy.
A "killed" mutant means at least one test failed — your tests caught the change.
A "surviving" mutant means all tests passed despite the code change — your tests missed this case.

mutation-score.good: Above 80% is generally considered good coverage quality
mutation-score.rule: High line coverage with a low mutation score means your tests run the code but don't actually verify behavior.

when-to-run.rule: Run mutation testing on critical business logic modules, not on the entire codebase (too slow).
Use it to identify gaps in tests for modules where correctness is most important: payment calculation, authorization logic, data validation.

builder-pattern.description: Use a fluent builder to construct test objects. Starts with sensible defaults, lets each test customize only what it cares about.

object-mother.description: A factory class that provides pre-built test objects for common scenarios. Simpler than builders for objects that don't need much variation.

avoid-magic-numbers.rule: Don't use unexplained literals in assertions: Assert.Equal(42, result). Use named constants or make the calculation visible.

database-tests.rule: Use in-memory databases (SQLite, H2, EF Core InMemory) for integration tests where possible — faster and no cleanup needed.
If you must test against a real database, use a test-specific database. Never run tests against a production or shared dev database.
Reset database state between tests. Either truncate tables in teardown, or wrap each test in a transaction and roll it back.
Seed only the data each test needs — don't share a large global seed fixture across all tests.

external-services.rule: Stub external HTTP services using tools like WireMock, Wiremock.NET, or nock. Never call real external services in unit or integration tests.
Record-and-replay (VCR cassettes) is an alternative to hand-written stubs for complex external APIs.
Define stubs at the HTTP level, not at the client class level — this tests your HTTP client code too.

coverage.rule: Target 80%+ line coverage on business logic. Don't pursue 100% for its own sake.
High coverage is necessary but not sufficient. Tests that don't assert anything can achieve 100% coverage while catching nothing.
Focus coverage effort on: business rules, validation logic, edge cases in calculations, authorization checks.
Don't chase coverage on: generated code, simple DTOs, framework boilerplate, trivial CRUD with no logic.
Branch coverage (was each true/false branch hit?) is more meaningful than line coverage.
